clips.title: AWS VPC & Subnets For Beginners
clips.why: A calm, visual explanation of what a VPC is, from a teacher who draws it as he talks.
look: The VPC as your own private network inside AWS, with an address range you pick.
Subnets are created later in the same video (the chapter "Creating Subnets"); in this lesson you cut them with cidrsubnet instead.
clips.after: Our sandbox VPC is exactly this picture with 10.60.0.0/16, cut into three subnets for VMs and one spare block for the proxy.

clips.title: Understanding RouteTables in AWS
clips.why: Route tables explained on their own, with a private subnet's table first, which is the one our sandboxes use.
look: The local route that every VPC route table has, so machines inside the VPC can reach each other.
What a private subnet's table is missing compared with a public one.
Stop after the private subnet part; the public subnet's internet route is the one we never add.
clips.after: A sandbox subnet's table is the private one, minus even the NAT route: local, plus the S3 endpoint.

clips.title: AWS VPC ENDPOINT | INTERFACE ENDPOINT | GATEWAY ENDPOINT | Simplified Visually
clips.why: The two kinds of endpoint, drawn side by side: a network card with a private address, and a route to S3.
look: The interface endpoint as a network card inside your subnet, reached through private DNS.
The gateway endpoint as an entry in the route table, only for S3 and DynamoDB.
Which of the two costs money, and which one is free.
clips.after: The sandbox VPC uses both: interface endpoints so the SSM agent can get commands, and a gateway endpoint, limited to our buckets, for S3.

practice.q: The sandbox VPC is 10.60.0.0/16, cut into four equal blocks. Complete the size of each block.
practice.hint: Two extra fixed bits on top of /16 make four blocks.
practice.why: Each extra fixed bit halves the block. /16 has 65,536 addresses, /17 has 32,768, and /18 has 16,384, so four /18 blocks fill the /16.

practice.q: Which route makes a subnet public?

options.why: Every VPC route table has this route. It only lets machines inside the VPC reach each other.
The default route to an internet gateway is the road to and from the internet. The sandbox subnets never get it.

options.text: An S3 prefix list (pl-...) to a VPC endpoint
options.why: That route only covers S3's addresses, and the traffic stays inside AWS.

practice.q: The SSM agent on a sandbox VM connects to ssm.us-east-1.amazonaws.com. With an interface endpoint and private DNS on, where does that name point?

options.text: To a private address of the endpoint's network card in the VM's own subnet
options.why: Private DNS makes the public service name resolve to the endpoint inside the VPC, which the local route already reaches.

options.text: To the public address of Systems Manager, through a hidden NAT
options.why: There is no hidden NAT. Without the endpoint the name would point to a public address the VM cannot reach.

options.text: To the egress proxy, which forwards it to AWS
options.why: The proxy is for the few outside sites on its allow-list. AWS services are reached through endpoints.

practice.q: Put the steps of building the sandbox network in order.
items: Plan the address range and cut it into blocks with cidrsubnet
Create one subnet per availability zone from the first three blocks
Check that the route table has only the local route and that there is no internet gateway
Add the S3 gateway endpoint with a policy for our bucket, and the interface endpoints for SSM
practice.why: Addresses come first, because subnets cannot be resized. Checking the empty route table before adding endpoints shows that every later route is one you added on purpose.

practice.q: Root on a sandbox VM tries to add a default route to the VM's own route table. Can that create a way out?

options.text: Yes, root can change any route
options.why: Root can change the route table inside the VM, but the subnet's route table lives in AWS, not on the machine.

options.text: No, because the subnet's route table in AWS still has no road out, and the VM's role cannot change it
options.why: AWS enforces the subnet's routes in its own network. A route inside the VM only points at a gateway that does not exist.

options.text: Only if it also opens port 443 in the security group
options.why: The VM cannot change its security group either, and even an open group needs a route to go anywhere.
